name: The Thermohaline Circulation
statement: Density differences from heat and salt drive a slow, globe-spanning overturning of the oceans.
meaning: The thermohaline circulation is the large-scale, density-driven part of global ocean circulation. Its name combines temperature and salt content, the two properties that set seawater density. Cold, salty and therefore dense water forms and sinks at high latitudes, flows through the deep ocean basins, and upwells elsewhere, forming a globe-spanning overturning loop, popularly the conveyor belt, that redistributes heat, salt, dissolved carbon, and nutrients. It is one of the fundamental engines of the climate system, distinct from but interwoven with the wind-driven surface currents.
mechanism: Deep water forms where surface water becomes dense enough to sink. In the far North Atlantic, cooling and evaporation make North Atlantic Deep Water that sinks and flows south; around Antarctica, brine rejected during sea-ice formation makes even denser Antarctic Bottom Water that flows along the sea floor. This sunken water travels slowly through the deep basins and eventually upwells, driven by mixing and by winds especially in the Southern Ocean, so a full overturning circuit takes on the order of a thousand years. The Atlantic limb, the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, carries the northward heat that keeps northwest Europe mild.

examples.text: North Atlantic Deep Water sinking in the Nordic and Labrador Seas, and Antarctic Bottom Water sinking around Antarctica, are the two great sites where surface water becomes dense enough to plunge into the deep ocean.
The Atlantic overturning carries northward heat that keeps northwest Europe relatively warm, accounting for much of the Atlantic's poleward heat transport.
The Younger Dryas cold reversal is linked to a pulse of glacial meltwater freshening the North Atlantic, inhibiting deep-water formation and weakening the overturning.

variants.name: The Atlantic overturning
variants.text: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, the Atlantic limb whose northward heat transport moderates European climate and which is the climatically vulnerable component.

variants.name: The wind-driven Gulf Stream
variants.text: A distinct, mainly wind-driven surface current; though popularly linked to the conveyor, it would keep flowing even if the overturning weakened, so the two must not be conflated.

whyItMatters: The circulation redistributes vast amounts of heat, moderating the climate of northern Europe, and it sequesters carbon by carrying dissolved carbon dioxide into the deep ocean for centuries while transporting the nutrients that support marine life. It is central to paleoclimate, where abrupt events like the Younger Dryas are read as overturning shutdowns driven by freshwater. And it is a focus of present concern, since a warming, freshening North Atlantic could weaken the Atlantic overturning, a low-probability but high-impact tipping point.

working.text: trace the circulation from where cold, salty water sinks to where it slowly upwells, driven by temperature and salt, not wind.
distinguish the density-driven overturning that carries heat northward from the wind-driven surface currents like the Gulf Stream.
expect added freshwater from ice melt to lower surface density and inhibit the sinking that drives the Atlantic overturning.

limits: The core physics is established, but future changes are uncertain and debated. Models and evidence suggest the Atlantic overturning is likely to weaken this century as freshwater from melting ice and warming reduce surface density; the assessed consensus is a very likely decline but only medium confidence that it will not collapse abruptly before 2100, so a full collapse is judged unlikely yet cannot be ruled out. Collapse timing is genuinely contested, with some studies warning of an earlier collapse and others finding greater resilience, and known model biases and incomplete meltwater representation limit confidence.
misreadings: The conveyor belt is a deliberate simplification, a cartoon of a far more complex, three-dimensional, turbulent, eddying system, not a single narrow tube of water. It is not one narrow current but a spatially distributed overturning involving basin-wide processes and Southern Ocean upwelling. And the popular scenario in which the Gulf Stream shuts down and freezes Europe overnight is exaggerated: the Gulf Stream is wind-driven and will not switch off, and even a significant weakening of the overturning would bring regional cooling over decades, not an instant ice age.
origin: The 'great ocean conveyor belt' concept and its iconic diagram were popularised by the climate scientist Wallace Broecker in the 1980s, with the two-layer schematic introduced with Tsung-Hung Peng in 1982 and the classic account in his 1991 paper 'The Great Ocean Conveyor'.

sources.text: Broecker, 'The Great Ocean Conveyor,' Oceanography 4(2) (1991): 79-89. — the conveyor-belt concept and the density-driven overturning.
